title: The Cards Reversed: a Print-Seller of Les Halles Invents Ancient Egypt
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Église Saint-Eustache, Paris: the birth in the market parish
stops.date_confidence: Year attested from the birth certificate (en.wikipedia, 'Etteilla'). The day is not. English Wikipedia's lead gives 1 March, its own body text says only 'his birth in Paris in 1738', and Wikidata records the birth with year precision only while giving the death full day precision. The day here is the lead's assertion, carried with that warning.
stops.campa: In the parish that serves the market halls a son is born into the Paris food trades: the father a maître rôtisseur, the mother a marchande grainière selling seed and grain. The registers give the year and the city; the day is another matter, and so is the name. English Wikipedia calls him Jean-Baptiste Alliette, German Wikipedia and Wikidata call him Jean-François, and the two are left standing where they stand. Saint-Eustache is the parish the family trades imply. No baptismal register naming it was reproduced in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Saint-Eustache, Les Halles, for 1738, not reproduced in any source consulted this session
sources: Wikidata Q317692 (P569 year precision; P735 Jean-François)

stops.name: Marché des Halles, Paris: the grain stalls of the childhood
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source dates any event of his youth; the year here is a placeholder inside the childhood that the 1738 birth implies.
stops.campa: He grows up among the grain and seed stalls, in the loudest commercial quarter of the city, where the price of bread is a public fact and the flour that feeds Paris changes hands in the open. The seed trade is his mother's and will be his own until he is thirty. No document places the boy in the market: the trade is attested, the childhood inside it is inference. Nothing in the record fixes a school, a master, a first employment, or the name of a single companion of these years.
suggested_refs: General histories of the Paris grain trade and the Halles market quarter under Louis XV

stops.name: Quai de la Mégisserie, Paris: the seed trade along the river
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the date is the weakest thing on this pin. No consulted source dates his entry into the seed trade; fr.wikipedia hedges even the trade itself with the conditional 'il aurait d'abord été, comme sa mère, marchand grainier', and hedges the exit as 'environ 1768'.
stops.campa: Along the riverside strip where seed, grain and produce change hands, he works his mother's trade. The sources agree he was a seed merchant before he was anything else, and agree on nothing further: not the year he began, not the shop, not whether he ever kept one of his own. The quay is the trade's usual ground, offered here as siting rather than as address. French Wikipedia will not even state the trade flat, writing that he would first have been a grain merchant like his mother. A decade of his working life carries no dated event at all.
suggested_refs: The riverside seed and grain trade of the Quai de la Mégisserie, standard ground of the trade in this reign

stops.name: Rouen: the meeting with Lecomte, called the Traveler
stops.date_confidence: The year 1757 is his own, printed by him in 1785; no independent corroboration exists. The month and day are unrecorded and defaulted here.
stops.campa: Twenty-eight years later he writes the meeting down: at Rouen, in 1757, a Parisian named Lecomte, nicknamed the Traveler, finds him occupied with French card-fortunetelling and tells him of a man who does as much with large cards. Large cards means tarot. The whole Egyptian edifice he will build begins, on his own account, with a stranger's remark in a Norman town. The account is his, published in the second cahier of 1785, and no other source corroborates the meeting, the man, or the year. The transcription below is reproduced as posted, spelling and all.
stops.quote: Erant à Rouen, en 1757, je fis la connoissance d'un nommé Lecomte, Parisien, surnommé le Voyageur; & sur ce qui'il me vis occupé à la Cartonomancie Francoise, il me dis qu'il connoissoit un Homme qui en faisoit autant que moi, avec de grandes Cartes.
stops.quote_source: Etteilla, 2nd Cahier (1785), as transcribed by commenter Steve Mangan in the discussion thread of Sherryl E. Smith, 'Was Etteilla Influenced by Piedmont Tarot?', Tarot Heritage blog (2015); the original cahier was not examined this session
suggested_refs: The 2nd cahier of Manière de se récréer avec le jeu de cartes nommées tarots (1785), containing his account of Rouen
sources: Tarot Heritage blog, 'Was Etteilla Influenced by Piedmont Tarot?' (2015), comment thread transcription

stops.name: Lamballe, Brittany: the teacher who cannot be found
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Tarot literature dates the apprenticeship 1757 to 1765; the year here sits in the middle of that span and rests on his own later account only.
stops.campa: The trail from Lecomte's remark leads, in his telling, into Brittany and to a man named Alexis who reads the large cards. Later tarot literature repeats an English phrase for this teacher, an aged Piedmontese, and dates the study 1757 to 1765. The phrase could not be traced this session to any verified translation, and the man could not be traced at all. What the record holds is a claim of eight years of apprenticeship, made by the student himself, decades afterward, inside a book selling the method he says he learned.
suggested_refs: The Lamballe episode as reported in tarot-history literature; no primary document for Alexis was located
sources: Sherryl E. Smith, 'Was Etteilla Influenced by Piedmont Tarot?', Tarot Heritage blog (2015)

stops.name: Paris, parish unnamed: the marriage to Jeanne Vattier
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (en.wikipedia); month and day unrecorded and defaulted. The location is a placeholder in central Paris, not a verified church.
stops.campa: He marries Jeanne Vattier. The marriage is attested and nothing around it is: no parish, no church, no witnesses, no month, no separation act, though the sources say the marriage lasted about five years. The pin sits at a placeholder because no consulted source names the building. A middle name, Jeanne-Vincente, circulates in one description of this event and appears in nothing consulted here; it is set aside rather than carried forward. He is twenty-five and selling seed, and will be selling prints by the time the marriage ends.
suggested_refs: Paris marriage registers for 1763, parish unidentified in any source consulted

stops.name: Pont Notre-Dame and Quai de Gesvres, Paris: the turn to prints
stops.date_confidence: The year is given as 'environ 1768' by fr.wikipedia; the site is a reconstruction from the standard geography of the eighteenth-century Paris print trade, not an attested address.
stops.campa: Around 1768 he stops selling seed and starts selling prints. The bridge shops of the Pont Notre-Dame and the quays beside them are where the Paris print and book trade lives in this reign, so this is the milieu a new marchand d'estampes enters; his own stall is documented nowhere. He is about thirty when the trade changes. A man who sold things that grow begins selling printed images, and within two years he is printing images of his own and telling the buyers what they mean.
suggested_refs: The print and book shops of the Pont Notre-Dame quarter before the bridge houses were cleared

stops.name: Paris, the shop of Lesclapart: the first book on the cards
stops.date_confidence: Imprint year attested: Amsterdam; Paris, Lesclapart, 1770. No month is printed.
stops.campa: The book appears with an Amsterdam imprint, a Paris seller named Lesclapart, and a title carrying the word Etteilla, his own surname reversed. The author line carries no name at all: par M.***, three asterisks. The reversed name is in the title before it is ever a signature. Inside is printed instruction in reading ordinary playing cards for the future, spreads and reversed meanings included, sold as a cure for boredom rather than as a revelation. English Wikipedia credits this book, not the later tarot volumes, with introducing card spreads and reversed positions.
stops.quote: L'amusement que je vous offre est, sans contredit, le tombeau de l'ennui, l'ame de la réflexion, le pere des conseils, le plaisir de la société.
stops.quote_source: Etteilla, ou manière de se récréer avec un jeu de cartes (Amsterdam/Paris, 1770), 'Au Lecteur', digitized copy, Internet Archive item 1770etteillaoumaniere; long-s normalized in transcription
suggested_refs: Etteilla, ou manière de se récréer avec un jeu de cartes, par M.*** (Amsterdam; Paris: Lesclapart, 1770)

stops.name: Paris, Au Lecteur: sixteen years of mastery claimed
stops.date_confidence: Same 1770 imprint as the preceding stop; the February date is a device to hold the two apart in sequence and carries no source of its own.
stops.campa: In the same preface he dates his own practice backward: sixteen years at the cards, which would set the beginning near 1754, three years before the meeting at Rouen he will describe in 1785. He is thirty-two and already claims to have been the master of the men and women who have made the most noise in the art. No independent record of that teaching exists. The claim is his, printed, and it is the first evidence that he means to be understood as a master of something rather than a shopkeeper with a hobby.
stops.quote: j'ose avouer que depuis 16 ans j'ai été le maître de ceux & de celles qui ont fait le plus de bruit en ce genre.
stops.quote_source: Etteilla, ou manière de se récréer avec un jeu de cartes (1770), preface, Internet Archive item 1770etteillaoumaniere
suggested_refs: The 'Au Lecteur' preface of the 1770 edition, earliest self-dating of his practice

stops.name: Amsterdam: the imprint that is not a journey
stops.date_confidence: The imprint is attested on the 1770 title page; the month is a sequencing device. No date, and no journey, attaches to Alliette in the Dutch Republic in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The title page says Amsterdam. French printers of this reign use foreign imprints routinely, to blunt the censor and to lend a book a cosmopolitan address it never had. No source consulted places Alliette in the Dutch Republic in this or any year. The pin marks a line of type rather than a stop on a road. It is the only foreign place his printed work claims for itself, and the claim belongs to the conventions of the trade, not to the biography of a man who appears never to have left the Paris region.
suggested_refs: Eighteenth-century French false imprints, 'A Amsterdam', as a censorship convention
sources: Standard bibliography of French false imprints; interpretation flagged as reconstruction

stops.name: Paris, chez Lesclapart: the sky, then the only way
stops.date_confidence: Two attested imprints held in one stop: Le Zodiaque mystérieux, ou les oracles d'Etteilla (1772) and Etteilla, ou la seule manière de tirer les cartes (1773). The pin carries the earlier year.
stops.campa: Two years after the card book he extends the method upward, into the sky: Le Zodiaque mystérieux, ou les oracles d'Etteilla. The year after that he revises and reissues the cards as Etteilla, ou la seule manière de tirer les cartes. Seule, the only way; the commercial voice of the enterprise arrives ahead of any doctrine. Lesclapart prints these too, and the widow Lesclapart will print the tarot book fifteen years on. Three books in four years, all on divination, by a man whose trade is still selling other people's engravings.
suggested_refs: Le Zodiaque mystérieux, ou les oracles d'Etteilla (1772); Etteilla, ou la seule manière de tirer les cartes (1773)

stops.name: Palais-Royal, Paris: the marketplace of fortune-tellers
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, siting and year both. His practice as consultant and teacher through the 1770s is described in general terms; no lease, tax roll or shop record for Alliette at the Palais-Royal was found this session.
stops.campa: Through the decade he builds a paying practice as a reader of cards and a teacher of the reading. The galleries of the Palais-Royal are, in these years, the busiest market in Paris for fortune-tellers, print-sellers and occult goods, and the setting historians of tarot place him in. Nothing consulted this session documents him there in particular. The practice is attested in general terms and undocumented in every particular: no client's name, no fee, no address, no year, no room.
suggested_refs: The commerce in fortune-telling and occult goods in the Palais-Royal galleries, 1770s and 1780s
sources: General histories of Palais-Royal commerce; specific documentation for Alliette not found

stops.name: Paris, the circle of Court de Gébelin: Le Monde primitif
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested. The quotation attached is not his own sentence: it is a posthumous editor's third-person summary printed about 1900, dating his restoration of the cards to about 1780.
stops.campa: Antoine Court de Gébelin publishes the eighth volume of Le Monde primitif and announces that the tarot deck is a surviving fragment of ancient Egypt, a Book of Thoth carried west. Alliette folds the claim into his own system and then disputes its ownership, insisting he had reached Egypt first and by himself. Later writers assign the priority according to which man they admire. No record of who thought it first survives; only the record of who said so, and both said so, in the same city, within a few years of each other.
stops.quote: Ce n'est qu'après trente ans de recherches et vers l'année 1780, que le fameux Etteilla les rétablit dans leur état primitif, et en expliqua les secrets à la manière des Egyptiens.
stops.quote_source: Le Grand Etteilla, ou l'Art de tirer les cartes, posthumous popular edition (Paris, c. 1900), Internet Archive item 1900legrandetteilla; editorial third person, not Etteilla's own words
suggested_refs: Antoine Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif, vol. VIII (1781), the essay on the tarot

stops.name: Paris, rue Thévenot: a girl who will keep soothsayers
stops.date_confidence: The address and years are attested in the atlas file empress_josephine.journey.json (rue Thévenot and Penthemont, 1781 to 1784). The month is a sequencing device. The connection to Etteilla is milieu, not contact.
stops.campa: By the early 1780s he is teaching the cards for money out of rented rooms, charging a fee per lesson and building a following among Parisians willing to pay a former seed merchant for a system he claims descends from ancient Egypt. No student list survives, no address for the lessons beyond the print quarter, no record of what a session actually cost. What survives is the printed system itself, sold to whoever can read and afford it, and the society he is already building around it to keep the teaching from scattering after him.
suggested_refs: Etteilla's paid card-reading lessons in the print quarter, early 1780s

stops.name: Paris: the loto des Indiens and the professor of algebra
stops.date_confidence: Imprint year attested for both titles. Note the second is Instruction sur la combinaison hislérique, extraite du Loto des Indiens, hislérique and not hystérique, in both the English and French articles.
stops.campa: Two instruction manuals appear, one on the loto des Indiens and one on what the title page calls the combinaison hislérique, and with them a title he keeps: Mr Etteilla, professeur d'algèbre. It is printed, not merely rumored, and it stands on the title page of a book about telling fortunes by lottery numbers. Whether any institution ever taught him algebra, or certified him in it, no consulted source says. French Wikipedia records that he presented himself the same way inside his own Tarot.
suggested_refs: Instruction sur le loto des Indiens que nous a donné en 1772 Mr Etteilla, professeur d'algèbre (1782)

stops.name: Paris, the presses of Segault and Legras: the first cahiers
stops.date_confidence: 1783 attested for the first and third cahiers and for L'Homme à projets. The often-quoted span 1783 to 1785 is contested: de.wikipedia gives 1783 to 1784, and no part of the work bears a 1784 imprint at all.
stops.campa: The first and third cahiers of Manière de se récréer avec le jeu de cartes nommées tarots are printed in Paris by Segault and Legras, with Mérigot and the author himself on the first, alongside L'Homme à projets. The title page names him l'auteur de la Cartonomancie, the word he coined for reading cards. Later literature treats this work as the standard reference of tarot cartomancy. Legras appears on no imprint of his after this year, and the second and fourth cahiers will not follow until 1785.
suggested_refs: Manière de se récréer avec le jeu de cartes nommées tarots, premier and troisième cahiers (Paris: l'auteur, Mérigot, Legras, Segault, 1783)

stops.name: Paris: the open letter to Court de Gébelin
stops.date_confidence: Imprint year attested; no month printed. This is the only imprint of his career dated 1784.
stops.campa: He publishes an Épître addressed to M. Court de Gébelin: an open letter from a print-seller to a member of the learned academies, arguing the tarot with him in public and signing off, at the end, salut, Etteilla. The name is a signature now and not only a word in a title. Both the English and French articles list the letter; neither reports what its addressee answered, and no reply was found this session. It is the only imprint of his life dated to this year.
suggested_refs: Épître à M. Court de Gébelin (1784)

stops.name: The Louvre, Paris: the commission that examined Mesmer
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the atlas file mesmer.journey.json: report to the King, 11 August 1784. The juxtaposition with Etteilla is this file's, not a source's.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of August a royal commission carrying Benjamin Franklin, Antoine Lavoisier and Jean Sylvain Bailly reports to the King that Mesmer's animal magnetism has no fluid behind it. The most fashionable invisible force in Paris is examined by the state and found empty. Half a mile east a man is selling an ancient Egyptian priesthood in a deck of cards and is subjected to no inquiry whatever, no commission, no royal report, nothing but customers who keep paying.
suggested_refs: The 1784 royal commission report on animal magnetism, Franklin, Lavoisier, Bailly

stops.name: Paris, chez l'auteur: the year he becomes his own publisher
stops.date_confidence: 1785 attested for the second and fourth cahiers, for Fragment sur les hautes sciences, and for Philosophie des hautes sciences.
stops.campa: The second and fourth cahiers appear with a different line at the foot of the page: Paris, chez l'auteur. He is his own publisher now. Two more books come the same year, the Fragment sur les hautes sciences and the Philosophie des hautes sciences, the second carrying six booksellers including Segaut. A third title often listed for 1785, L'Astrologie du Livre de Toth, turns out under inspection to be the name of a 1993 reprint of the fourth cahier; it is absent from the French bibliography entirely, and is dropped here.
suggested_refs: Philosophie des hautes sciences (Amsterdam; Paris: l'auteur, Nyon l'aîné, Durand neveu, Mérigot le jeune, Segaut, 1785)

stops.name: Alexandria: the library that burned and the book that escaped
stops.date_confidence: The claim is his, made in the 1780s; the exact month is a sequencing device. The wording quoted comes from a posthumous Paris edition of about 1900 reporting him in the third person, not from a volume he published.
stops.campa: The claim, as a posthumous popular edition reports it, runs like this: the Book of Thoth was seventy-eight leaves of the purest gold, hieroglyphs traced on them, explained aloud each day within the family by its head, and it is, he says, the only book that escaped the fury of Omar when the library of Alexandria burned. The pin sits on the library because the claim requires it there. No Egyptian source names a tarot, and none will when the writing is finally read, fifteen years after his death.
stops.quote: il est, dit-il, le seul livre qui soit échappé à la fureur d'Omar, lorsqu'il fit incendier la célèbre bibliothèque d'Alexandrie.
stops.quote_source: Le Grand Etteilla, ou l'Art de tirer les cartes, posthumous popular edition (Paris, c. 1900), Internet Archive item 1900legrandetteilla
suggested_refs: Le Grand Etteilla, ou l'Art de tirer les cartes (Paris, c. 1900), reporting the Egyptian origin claim

stops.name: Paris: the preface that denies the lodges
stops.date_confidence: Conjectural year. The title page carries no date: en.wikipedia gives the imprint as s.l. [Paris], s.d. [1786], so 1786 is a cataloguer's bracket rather than a printed year.
stops.campa: In a preface to Les Sept nuances de l'oeuvre philosophique-hermétique he does what the century's occultists rarely do: he denies being a Freemason. He grants true Masonry the respect any Brother could have for it and dismisses the little denominations of Lodges and grades as more folly than wisdom. He is building a fraternity of his own by now and wants it understood as a separate thing, declining the borrowed builder's myth of Hiram Abiff and the borrowed rose-and-cross of Christian Rosenkreuz alike, in a city full of men claiming both.
stops.quote: pour tout ce qui est de vraie Maçonnerie, autant de respect que puisse en avoir un Frère
stops.quote_source: Etteilla, 'Petit avant-propos pour le denier du pauvre', in Les Sept nuances de l'oeuvre philosophique-hermétique (1786), quoted with citation in Wikipedia (fr), 'Etteilla'; the original volume was not examined this session
suggested_refs: Les Sept nuances de l'oeuvre philosophique-hermétique, s.l. [Paris], s.d. [1786]

stops.name: Paris: the method spreads to faces and hands
stops.date_confidence: Year attested in the English publication list; no copy was examined this session and no detail of the contents is claimed here.
stops.campa: The method leaves the table and moves onto the body. He publishes on metoposcopy, the reading of foreheads, and on palmistry, applying to faces and hands the same procedure he applied to cards and to the zodiac: a fixed set of signs, a fixed set of meanings, and a fee for the reading. He is forty-nine and has now published on playing cards, tarot, the zodiac, lottery numbers, foreheads and hands, without once leaving the trade of selling printed paper in central Paris.
suggested_refs: The 1787 works on metoposcopy and chiromancy, listed in Wikipedia (en), 'Etteilla'

stops.name: Paris, the widow Lesclapart: Jeu des tarots, ou le livre de Thot
stops.date_confidence: Year attested. The quotation attached is a posthumous editor's third-person summary of the Egyptian claim, printed about 1900, not a sentence from this 1788 volume.
stops.campa: Jeu des tarots, ou le livre de Thot is issued by the widow Lesclapart, whose husband's shop sold his first book eighteen years earlier. Egypt is in the title now. The system has its origin myth, its vocabulary, its correspondences and its author's name working as a brand; what it does not have, and never will, is a single document older than the author. Between the pamphlet of 1770 and this book he has moved from teaching a parlour amusement to publishing a scripture, without changing trade, quarter or city.
stops.quote: C'est aux Égyptiens primitifs qu'Etteilla attribue l'invention des tarots ou livre de Thot: ce livre était composé de 78 lames de l'or le plus pur, sur lesquelles étaient tracées des hiéroglyphes, c'est-à-dire des figures mystérieuses, dont l'explication était faite tous les jours en famille, par leur chef.
stops.quote_source: Le Grand Etteilla, ou l'Art de tirer les cartes, posthumous popular edition (Paris, c. 1900), Internet Archive item 1900legrandetteilla; editorial summary in the third person
suggested_refs: Jeu des tarots, ou le livre de Thot (Paris: Mad. veuve Lesclapart, 1788)

stops.name: Paris, address unrecorded: the Société des Interprètes du Livre de Thot
stops.date_confidence: Year attested in the English article and in general tarot-history literature; the month is a sequencing device. No meeting address, membership list or rule survives in anything consulted.
stops.campa: He founds the Société des Interprètes du Livre de Thot. It has no lodge and no hall; it works by post, French-speaking readers sending interpretations to one another and to him. It is the first association organized around reading tarot, and he is fifty the year he founds it. No consulted source gives a meeting address, a membership list, or a rule of the body. The body is a lodge without a building, set up two years after its founder denied in print that he belonged to any lodge at all.
suggested_refs: Correspondence of the Société des Interprètes du Livre de Thot, no archive located this session

stops.name: Paris, engraver unnamed: the deck called the Grand Etteilla
stops.date_confidence: Sources disagree: fr.wikipedia dates the printing across 1788 and 1789 ('En 1788-89, il fit imprimer sa version du Tarot'), while the English and German articles give 1789 flat. The engraver and workshop are unrecorded.
stops.campa: He has a deck of his own cut and printed: seventy-eight cards, the Marseille pattern crossed with Egyptian figures, made to be read rather than played. Collectors will name three patterns after him, the Grand Etteilla of seventy-eight cards, the Petit Etteilla of thirty-two, the Nouvel Etteilla of fifty-four. A purpose-built divination deck for the amusement of ladies was registered in Paris in April 1788, so his is the first tarot made for divination, not the first divining deck. The French and English articles disagree on the year.
suggested_refs: Surviving Grand Etteilla sheets and early impressions; the Jeu de cartomancie pour l'amusement des dames, registered 15 April 1788

segments.name: The Revolution and the Last School

stops.name: Place de la Bastille, Paris: the fortress falls a mile east
stops.date_confidence: Attested date, taken with the coordinate from marques_de_lafayette.journey.json. Alliette's own presence or absence that day is unrecorded.
stops.campa: The fortress falls a mile east of the print quarter. The guilds that structure the print trade are about to be dissolved and the censor's office with them, and the market for printed prophecy is about to become a market for printed politics. No consulted source records where Alliette was that day, what he made of it, or whether the upheaval touched his practice at all. His own society keeps meeting regardless, teaching a system built to outlast kings and censors both, and for a while it does.
suggested_refs: The fall of the Bastille, 14 July 1789, and its effect on the Paris print trade

stops.name: Paris: the Cours théorique et pratique du livre de Thot
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; no month printed. The attribution of the Major and Minor Arcana division to this volume comes from the English article and is not traced here to a page of the original.
stops.campa: His fullest statement of the method assigns each card its correspondences, planets and signs and the four classical elements, and divides the deck into the two groups later writers will call the Major and Minor Arcana. The scheme outlives every claim it was built to support. Two centuries of tarot books inherit the architecture from this volume and the Egypt from the volume before it, mostly without knowing whose architecture they are using or that it was assembled by a print-seller in the second year of the Revolution.
suggested_refs: Cours théorique et pratique du livre de Thot (1790)

stops.name: Paris, address unrecorded: the Nouvelle École de Magie
stops.date_confidence: Full date attested in the English article: founded 1 July 1790. The address, the enrollment and the curriculum are recorded nowhere consulted.
stops.campa: On the first of July he founds the Nouvelle École de Magie and prints its prospectus, the Aperçu sur la nouvelle école de magie. A school of magic opens in Paris in the summer after the Bastille, run by a fifty-two year old seller of engravings who calls himself a professor of algebra. The date is exact in the sources and everything else about the school is missing: where it met, who enrolled, what was taught, whether it survived its founder by a single day.
suggested_refs: Aperçu sur la nouvelle école de magie (1790)

stops.name: Paris: the Journal projetique et patriotique
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; no month printed and no run of issues located this session.
stops.campa: The last title of his life is a periodical, the Journal projetique et patriotique. Patriotique is a Revolutionary word and it is now on his masthead; projetique reaches back to L'Homme à projets of 1783, a phrase he had already used for himself. The man who spent twenty years publishing on cards, stars, numbers and hands ends by publishing on the state of France. No copy was examined this session. What he actually said about the Revolution in it is a gap.
suggested_refs: Journal projetique et patriotique (1791), no surviving run located this session

stops.name: Paris, house unnamed: the death on the twelfth of December
stops.date_confidence: Attested across the English and French articles and carried at full day precision by Wikidata, which is more than the birth receives.
stops.campa: He dies in Paris on the twelfth of December, fifty-three years old. The date is firm across every source, which is more than can be said for the day he was born. The house is not named, the cause is not given, no will or inventory is cited, and nothing consulted says who was with him. His wife, if she was living, goes unmentioned; the marriage had ended in separation twenty-three years before and no source follows her afterward. The society met by post and the school met nowhere on record. The death is a date without a room.
suggested_refs: Paris death registers for December 1791, not reproduced in any source consulted

stops.name: Paris, burial place unknown: the grave that is not recorded
stops.date_confidence: The burial itself is undated and unlocated. The date here is a placeholder in the days after the attested death; treat any claimed tomb site as unverified.
stops.campa: No cemetery, tomb or grave is named for him in anything consulted: not the French or English encyclopedia articles, not the BnF authority record, not the Find a Grave memorial, which carries no burial location at all. The parish cemeteries of the old regime were being closed and moved in exactly these years, which is an explanation rather than a record. The gap is written here as a gap. Nothing consulted names a mourner, a cost, a parish, or a stone.
suggested_refs: Find a Grave memorial 270517479, carrying no burial location

stops.name: Les Halles, Paris: the whole life inside a few streets
stops.date_confidence: Synthesis of every dated fact in this file rather than an event. No travel outside the Paris region, except Rouen in 1757 and the Brittany episode he reports himself, is documented in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Read end to end, the record keeps him inside a few streets. Born in the market parish, selling seed by the river, selling prints by the bridge, teaching in rooms nobody wrote down the address of, dying at an address nobody wrote down either. The furthest he is documented to have gone is Rouen in 1757; the furthest his books go is Amsterdam on a title page and Alexandria in a legend. The journey of Etteilla covers a few square kilometres, and every other place in it is a claim about somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The Les Halles quarter as the fixed ground of the whole documented life
sources: Synthesis of all dated claims in this file

stops.name: Bibliothèque du Roi, rue de Richelieu, Paris: the books outlast the man
stops.date_confidence: Undated accession. The BnF authority record lists holdings of his works without giving dates of entry; the year here marks the period after his death, not a documented transfer.
stops.campa: His printed work survives institutionally. Copies of the cartomancy manuals, the tarot cahiers and the Book of Thoth treatise enter the royal library on the rue de Richelieu and stay there under the library's later names, listed now in the BnF authority record for Etteilla. Almost everything known about the man comes off these title pages, which is why his biography reads as a bibliography with a birth and a death fastened to the ends. No manuscript, letter or account book of his is recorded among them.
suggested_refs: data.bnf.fr authority record for Etteilla, listing surviving holdings

stops.name: Toulon: the fleet sails for the Egypt he invented
stops.date_confidence: Sailing date drawn from empress_josephine.journey.json; the Egypt campaign itself is anchored in napoleon.journey.json. The juxtaposition with Etteilla is this file's inference.
stops.campa: The fleet sails for Egypt and the campaign returns with the Description de l'Égypte. Seven years after Alliette's death, the Egypt he invented for a deck of cards becomes a country the French army measures, draws and catalogues, plate by plate, temple by temple. The savants aboard are the first Europeans to survey the place as evidence rather than as legend, and nothing in the volumes they bring back answers to a Book of Thoth in seventy-eight leaves of gold, a priesthood, or a deck of cards at all.
suggested_refs: The Description de l'Égypte, published from 1809, product of the savants of the 1798 campaign

stops.name: Rosetta: the stone that reads the hieroglyphs back
stops.date_confidence: Attested date of the find in pierre_francois_bouchard.journey.json. The connection drawn here to Etteilla's Egyptian claim is a juxtaposition made by this file, not by any source.
stops.campa: An officer of engineers named Pierre-François Bouchard, rebuilding a fort at Rosetta, turns up a slab carrying three scripts. Champollion will read the hieroglyphs from it, and Egyptian writing stops being a surface onto which anything can be projected. No Egyptian text found then or since mentions a deck of cards, a Book of Thoth in gold leaves, or a priesthood reading them daily. The foundation is taken out from under the system eight years after its author is buried in a grave no one recorded.
suggested_refs: The Rosetta Stone, found 16 July 1799, and Champollion's decipherment announced 1822

stops.name: Paris: Marie-Anne Lenormand and the claimed descent
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No date and no documented meeting are given anywhere consulted; the year is a marker for the generation after his death.
stops.campa: Marie-Anne Lenormand builds the most famous fortune-telling practice of the next generation on a method descended from his. Later tradition makes her his pupil. The claim comes mostly from her own advertising, and no record close to the events puts her in his rooms; she was a teenager in Paris during his last years, which is the whole of what the documentation supports. She becomes far better known than the man whose system she works inside, and her name is the one later readers remember when his own has already gone quiet.
suggested_refs: Nineteenth-century accounts of Lenormand's claimed apprenticeship, none contemporary with Etteilla

stops.name: Paris: the Petit Etteilla and the pseudonym Julia Orsini
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Julia Orsini reissues are dated only as early nineteenth century in general tarot-history literature and were not independently verified this session; no imprint was examined.
stops.campa: The Petit Etteilla manuals and decks keep printing in Paris under a shifting cast of publishers, and by the early nineteenth century the method is being reissued under a new pseudonym, Julia Orsini, for a wider and cheaper readership. The pseudonymous author of 1770 has become a pseudonymous franchise. The specific printers were not individually verified this session, and the Orsini attribution rests on general tarot-history literature rather than on any imprint examined here.
suggested_refs: The Julia Orsini cartomancy manuals, Paris, early nineteenth century
sources: General tarot-publishing history; not re-verified this session

stops.name: Paris: the cardmaking houses take the pattern
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, year included. The chain from Etteilla's own plates to the nineteenth-century manufacturers is inferred from the general history of French playing-card manufacture, not documented.
stops.campa: French cardmaking houses take up the pattern, the firm later known as Grimaud among them, and Etteilla decks are made at industrial scale for a market of readers the seed merchant's son would not recognize. The chain from his own plates to theirs is a reconstruction and not a documented descent. Downstream sits the deck most people now mean by tarot: Pamela Colman Smith's 1909 illustrations for Arthur Edward Waite, the next fully illustrated deck published under a named author's system.
suggested_refs: Nineteenth-century French Etteilla-pattern decks; the 1909 Rider-Waite-Smith deck as the successor lineage
sources: General history of French playing-card manufacture

stops.name: Paris: Éliphas Lévi calls the writings barbarous
stops.date_confidence: Contested. The wording quoted is from Waite's revised translation of Transcendental Magic, Doctrine ch. XXI, issued by Rider in 1923 and after; Waite's first translation of 1896 reads differently. The French sentence circulating for the same verdict carries no citation at all in fr.wikipedia, and the year is given as 1856 in one account and 1860 in another.
stops.campa: Éliphas Lévi, rebuilding French occultism a lifetime later, needs the tarot and does not want its first modern teacher. He calls the writings obscure, wearisome and barbarous in style, and elsewhere calls the man a former barber who never learned French or orthography. The trade is wrong: the record has him selling seed and then prints. Three of Lévi's sentences about him circulate in English in wordings that differ between Waite's 1896 translation and Waite's revised one, and the French article that relays the insult attaches no work, no page and no year.
stops.quote: The writings of Etteilla, now very rare, are obscure, wearisome and barbarous in style.
stops.quote_source: Éliphas Lévi, Transcendental Magic: Its Doctrine and Ritual, trans. A. E. Waite, revised Rider edition (1923 and reprints), Doctrine ch. XXI 'Divination', p. 164; verified in Internet Archive item eliphas-levi-transcendental-magic-its-doctrine-and-ritual
suggested_refs: Waite's two translations of Transcendental Magic, 1896 and the revised Rider text, which differ in this sentence
sources: Internet Archive item transcendentalma00leviuoft (1896, variant wording)

stops.name: Paris: the bastard deck, in the History of Magic
stops.date_confidence: The sentence belongs to Lévi's History of Magic, verified in Internet Archive items historyofmagicin00lv, eliphas-levi-the-history-of-magic and in.gov.ignca.7242, and not to Transcendental Magic as it is usually cited. The 1860 year and the 1856 year given elsewhere for the same verdict contradict each other and are left unresolved.
stops.campa: The judgment repeats in the History of Magic, where the charge is not fraud but incompetence: thirty years of labour producing a bastard set, the keys transposed, the numbers no longer answering to the signs. What Lévi objects to is that Alliette reordered the cards, which is the liberty Lévi takes himself. The two most quoted English sentences about Etteilla come from two different books by the same author in two different translations, and the sources that repeat them mostly say neither.
stops.quote: This illuminated hairdresser, after working for thirty years, only succeeded in producing a bastard set, the Keys of which are transposed, so that the numbers no longer answer to the signs.
stops.quote_source: Éliphas Lévi, The History of Magic, trans. A. E. Waite (London: Rider), Bk VI ch. V; verified in Internet Archive item historyofmagicin00lv (1922 printing)
suggested_refs: Éliphas Lévi, The History of Magic, Bk VI ch. V, on the Tarot and the gipsies

stops.name: Paris: Theosophy inherits the Egyptian claim
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Theosophical Society's 1875 founding is attested in blavatsky.journey.json; the lineage from Etteilla's Egyptian claim to it is drawn by this file and by no source consulted.
stops.campa: Helena Blavatsky's Theosophical Society takes the idea he was the first to fasten onto a deck of cards, that ancient Egyptian wisdom survives encoded in symbols, and carries it around the world in a far larger vehicle. The line runs from a print-seller through Lévi, who despised him, into a movement that never names him. The claim outlives both its author and its evidence, and it is repeated by people who have never heard of Les Halles.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society, founded 1875, and its Egyptian-wisdom lineage claims

stops.name: Paris: René Guénon takes the pedigree apart
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, year included. Guénon's critical writing on occultist origin myths is recorded in rene_guenon.journey.json; no source consulted names Etteilla in that criticism, and the year here marks the period of the critique rather than a dated statement about him.
stops.campa: René Guénon, writing in Paris against the occultists, treats the tarot's claimed Egyptian pedigree as a modern manufacture rather than an ancient inheritance. He works in the same city where the pedigree was manufactured a hundred and forty years earlier, closing a loop the sources never draw for themselves: the critic and the inventor breathing the same Paris air, a century and a half apart, one undoing in a chapter what the other built over a lifetime of decks and pamphlets.
suggested_refs: Guénon's writings on the errors of the occultists and on invented esoteric pedigrees

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the same object, made again
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Xul Solar and Ral Veroni are queue entries rather than researched files, and the year marks Xul Solar's Buenos Aires period loosely; no date is claimed for either deck here.
stops.campa: The line reaches the far side of the Atlantic and keeps going. Every deck built afterward for reading rather than for play, in whatever country and whatever cosmology, repeats the same basic move he made first: a standard pack reordered, renumbered, and sold with a printed key explaining what each card means. No document traces a single one of these later decks back to him by name. What connects them is the form itself, which he was the first to publish as a form and to sell with instructions.
suggested_refs: The tarot-as-reading-object form, published first by Etteilla and repeated without attribution ever since

stops.name: Issy-les-Moulineaux, Musée français de la carte à jouer: the trade keeps a museum
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The pin marks a standing institution at 16 rue Auguste-Gervais, not an event; the year is a placeholder. Coordinate taken from Wikidata rather than from the geography lens, which was about two hundred metres off.
stops.campa: A museum of playing cards stands at 16 rue Auguste-Gervais, holding more than eleven thousand sets, among them over seven thousand card games and more than a thousand prints, drawings and posters. Its own encyclopedia article never mentions Etteilla, and whether any Etteilla-pattern deck sits in its cases was not confirmed this session. The trade he entered by accident in 1768, printed images sold by the sheet, has a national collection a few kilometres from Les Halles. He is not named in it.
